newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch mull May summit to kick-start treaty reforms.
newsitem.headline: Dutch mull May summit to kick-start treaty reforms.

text.p: The Dutch EU presidency said on Wednesday it was still considering calling an extra summit of European Union heads of government to try and kick-start deadlocked talks on reforming the bloc's unwieldy institutions.

A foreign ministry spokesman in The Hague said EU foreign ministers would meet as scheduled in Luxembourg on April 29-30 and, depending on their progress, an extra summit could be called on May 23, probably in Maastricht, the southern Dutch town where the last EU treaty was brokered in late 1991.
"If we are going to call a special summit, we would probably do so at that (April 29-30) meeting," the spokesman said.

The year-long inter-governmental conference (IGC), aimed at wide-ranging treaty reforms to prepare the 15-member bloc for an ambitious eastward expansion, has become bogged down over how to re-shape the executive Commission and ensure a fair weighting of member states' votes in the decision-making process.
EU heads of government are due to meet in Amsterdam on June 16-17 to agree a new treaty, paving the way for accession talks with a number of ex-communist states from Eastern Europe.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok signalled in early March that his presidency was thinking about the need for a special summit.
A May 23 meeting would come three weeks after British elections, widely expected to oust the ruling Conservatives after 18 years in government.

The extra summit would give EU members a chance to size up the European credentials of a new British government. Many hope that a Labour Party victory would bring a more EU-friendly Tony Blair to the negotiating table, allowing some progress to be made on key issues such as social policy reforms.

The IGC talks have stumbled recently as the bloc's larger and smaller members are sharply divided over how many seats each should have on the Commission and how much weight each member's votes should carry when deciding on new policy.
Attempts to forge a common foreign policy have also been savaged by France's decision not to join an annual EU-sponsored motion condemning China's record on human rights.

The Dutch EU presidency had hoped to get full backing at a meeting of EU ministers in the coastal town of Noordwijk last weekend for an EU censure of China to be tabled at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva, but Paris, supported by Germany, Spain and Italy, broke ranks saying dialogue with China was better than confrontation.
That prompted Denmark to say it would table a resolution against China in Geneva this week. Beijing reacted sharply, warning Copenhagen that such a move would damage relations.

French Defence Minister Charles Millon, in China ahead of next month's visit by President Jacques Chirac, on Tuesday hailed Chinese moves towards accepting U.N. human rights standards and said he hoped an EU ban on arms sales to China could be lifted.
Military sales remain banned by the EU since China crushed student-led pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989.

China praised Paris for not joining the EU rights motion, hinting that this would boost French business with China. Europe's Airbus Industrie hopes to win a major order for planes during Chirac's visit.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo has warned his EU colleagues that the internal rift over the human rights motion could damage the EU's credibility on the world stage.
